title: On Writing About Home When Home Has Become Complicated
body:
The word 'home' does an enormous amount of work in memoir. It carries the weight of childhood, identity, belonging, loss — and when home is a place you have left or been separated from, or a place that no longer exists in the form you remember it, writing about it requires a specific kind of precision. Sentimentality is fatal. So is false resolution.

What I have found is that honest writing about a complicated home has to hold two things simultaneously: the genuine attachment to what was real and good, and the equally genuine reckoning with what was not. Readers recognise the tension between love and clarity. What they resist is the version that resolves it too easily.

title: The Problem With Writing About Real People
body:
Memoir is one of the few forms that takes real people as its material. This creates an ethical problem that does not have a clean resolution. The people in your story have their own version of events. They may be living. They may read what you have written. They did not consent to be characters.

The conventional advice — change identifying details, composite characters — only partially addresses this. The deeper question is about the relationship between your truth and theirs. Memoir is necessarily one perspective. It can acknowledge this without becoming relativism. 'This is what it was like for me' is not the same as 'this is what happened.' The distinction is worth making explicit.

title: What Tehran Taught Me About Truth and Silence
body:
There are cultures where the indirect approach to truth is not evasion but courtesy. Where saying the difficult thing directly is a failure of tact rather than a virtue of honesty. Growing up between Iranian and Western frameworks of communication meant spending a long time working out which register I was operating in at any given moment.

Writing about return — about going back to a place that shaped you, with adult eyes — involved navigating this constantly. What do I say directly? What is better left to implication? The memoir form prizes directness, personal disclosure, the nakedness of honest self-examination. This is not a universal value. Making peace with that tension was part of writing the book.

title: Displacement and the Question of Where You Belong
body:
The literature of displacement — migration narratives, exile memoirs, the stories of people who live between cultures — often ends with arrival. A sense of place found, belonging established. I am suspicious of this ending, not because it is never true, but because it is frequently too easy.

What displacement more often produces, in my experience, is a permanent bifocality. You see the new place through the eyes of someone who knows what elsewhere looks like. You see the old place through the eyes of someone who has been away. Neither view is simple. The 'where do you belong?' question, for people who have lived between places, often does not have a single honest answer.

title: Writing From the Body: How Memory Lives in the Physical
body:
Phenomenological memory — memory that lives in the body rather than the mind — is some of the most powerful material in memoir. The smell that returns you instantly to a childhood kitchen. The weight of a specific bag. The exact quality of light on a particular afternoon that you cannot quite explain knowing but know.

This kind of material resists summary. It has to be rendered, not reported. The craft of memoir is substantially the craft of finding language precise enough to convey a physical experience to someone who has not had it — of making the specific general through the depth of the particularity rather than through abstraction.

title: The Unreliable Narrator and the Honest Memoirist
body:
The narrator of any memoir is unreliable in the technical sense — they are a person whose perspective is limited, whose memory is fallible, whose emotional state at the time of writing colours what they see. This is not a flaw to be apologised for but a condition to be acknowledged and worked with.

The most honest memoirists are those who build their unreliability into the text. Not as a postmodern device, but as a genuine epistemic position: I may have misremembered this. I did not know then what I know now. The person who experienced this event is not quite the person writing about it. This kind of transparency creates trust rather than undermining it.

title: When the Story Has No Resolution
body:
Narrative convention demands resolution. Memoir, which takes its material from real life, is often working with material that has not resolved — where the grief is ongoing, the estrangement continues, the question that drove the book remains genuinely open. The temptation is to manufacture an ending that the real experience does not have.

The alternative — and I think it is more honest — is to find a way to end without resolving. To close the narrative while acknowledging that life continues beyond it. Some of the best memoirs end not with an answer but with a changed relationship to the question. The protagonist understands it differently, even if they cannot settle it. This is usually truer to experience than resolution.

title: Language, Translation, and the Stories We Cannot Quite Tell
body:
Some experiences resist translation not because language fails generally but because the specific language in which the experience occurred has connotations that do not carry over. There are Persian words for emotional states, for relational dynamics, for qualities of situation that have no English equivalent — not because English is poorer, but because the experiences they name are specific to a particular cultural context.

Writing memoir in a second language means deciding, constantly, whether to translate or to explain or simply to leave the gap visible. Sometimes the gap is the content. The absence of a word in the target language is evidence of the distance between the two worlds you are moving between.
